levels.title: Foundations
levels.tagline: Mindset, methodology, and the frameworks every later level assumes.
levels.description: Start here regardless of background. You'll learn how IR actually runs as a lifecycle, the order evidence disappears in, the frameworks (ATT&CK, Pyramid of Pain, Diamond Model) every later artifact page leans on without re-explaining, and how to write up findings two audiences can both use.

lessons.title: The Incident Response Lifecycle
lessons.summary: Preparation through lessons-learned as an actual operating cycle, not a poster on a wall -- and why skipping straight to eradication is the most common real-world mistake.
objectives: Name the six phases of the IR lifecycle in order and what each one actually produces
Explain why containment and eradication are distinct decisions, not one step
Identify the one phase most real incidents shortchange, and why that costs you later
Connect the lifecycle to where the rest of this academy's artifact lessons plug in

lessons.title: Order of Volatility
lessons.summary: Which evidence disappears first, and why collection order is a decision you make once, under pressure, with no do-overs.
objectives: Recall the RFC 3227 ordering and its practical enterprise collapse
Explain why network isolation is preferable to power-off in most cases
Extend the volatility concept to retention-limited log sources
Sequence a live response so irreversible steps happen first

lessons.title: MITRE ATT&CK Primer
lessons.summary: Tactics vs. techniques vs. sub-techniques, and how to read a technique ID (T1055.012) as more than a label -- the shared vocabulary every artifact page in this academy maps back to.
objectives: Distinguish tactics, techniques, and sub-techniques and read an ATT&CK ID
Explain why one technique can serve multiple tactics
Use the Data Sources section to identify instrumentation gaps
Explain why percentage coverage of ATT&CK is a misleading metric

lessons.title: Pyramid of Pain
lessons.summary: Why a hash is a cheap indicator and a TTP is an expensive one for the adversary to change -- and what that means for where you should actually invest detection effort.
objectives: Recall the six levels and the adversary cost associated with each
Explain why hash-based detection is cheap to build and cheap to evade
Explain why this academy phrases red flags as behaviors
Avoid the error of dismissing low-level indicators entirely

lessons.title: The Diamond Model
lessons.summary: Adversary, capability, infrastructure, victim -- the four vertices that turn a pile of indicators into an analyzable intrusion, with the pivoting logic that makes it useful mid-investigation.
objectives: Name the four vertices and the meta-features that link events
Execute the pivots that expand one indicator into a scoped incident
Explain why attribution is optional in enterprise IR
Position the Diamond Model alongside ATT&CK and the Kill Chain

lessons.title: Evidence Handling & Chain of Custody
lessons.summary: What actually needs documenting in enterprise IR (versus what's theater left over from criminal-prosecution workflows this academy isn't built for), and where hashing fits.
objectives: Distinguish admissibility from defensibility as operating standards
Identify the practices that are genuinely load-bearing in enterprise IR
Explain what a chain of custody means in an enterprise context
Recognize the handoff point where Legal must be involved

lessons.title: Timeline Construction & Correlation
lessons.summary: Building a super-timeline from multiple sources with different clocks, different precision, and the clock-skew calibration trick that makes cross-source correlation actually trustworthy.
objectives: Normalize multiple sources to UTC and state the timezone in reporting
Calibrate host clock skew using a cross-recorded event
Use pivot-and-expand rather than sequential reading
Corroborate a suspect $SI-based timeline against $FN and the USN journal

lessons.title: Operationalizing Threat Intelligence
lessons.summary: Turning a feed of indicators into something that actually changes what your SOC does today, not a PDF nobody opens.
objectives: Apply the test for whether intelligence is operational
Explain why new indicators require retrospective search
Explain why an aging policy prevents false positives against third parties
Explain why tactical-only consumption is the least durable approach

lessons.title: Building an ATT&CK Coverage Map
lessons.summary: Turning this academy's own artifact-by-artifact coverage into a single tactic-level view -- and why naming your own gaps openly is more useful than pretending you don't have any.
objectives: Score coverage by demonstrated capability rather than tool ownership
Distinguish the four honest coverage levels including validated detection
Treat vendor coverage layers as claims to test
Explain why a documented gap beats a flattering score

lessons.title: Reporting & Communication
lessons.summary: The same finding, written twice -- once for the engineer who has to fix it, once for the executive who has to decide something because of it -- and why conflating the two audiences is how good findings get ignored.
objectives: Write the same finding for technical and executive audiences
Lead with the answer rather than methodology or chronology
Apply consistent confidence language and never state hypotheses as fact
Document what could not be determined and why it matters

lessons.title: Sysmon Deployment & Configuration
lessons.summary: What Sysmon actually is, the event IDs referenced constantly across this academy, and how to deploy it without drowning in noise.
objectives: Explain what gap Sysmon fills beyond native Windows Event ID 4688
Map Sysmon Event IDs 1, 3, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 17/18, and 22 to the academy lessons that depend on each
Explain why an untuned default Sysmon configuration can be counterproductive
Identify why local-only Sysmon logs defeat much of their investigative value

levels.title: Windows Endpoint Forensics
levels.tagline: What ran, what touched disk, and what a normal machine looks like before you can spot an abnormal one.
levels.description: The core host-based artifact set: execution evidence (Prefetch, Shimcache, Amcache, UserAssist), the filesystem's own record of itself ($MFT, USN Journal), and the registry/process baseline everything else in this academy gets compared against.

lessons.title: Artifact: Prefetch
lessons.summary: Proof a program ran, when, how many times, and what files/DLLs it touched on first launch -- and the one registry key that silently turns this artifact off on servers.
objectives: Explain what a .pf file records and why the hash suffix encodes the executable path
Explain why an empty Prefetch directory on a server is expected rather than suspicious
Use the referenced-file list to characterize a since-deleted binary
State what Prefetch proves compared to Amcache and ShimCache

lessons.title: Artifact: $MFT & Timestomping
lessons.summary: MACB timestamps split across two attributes ($SI and $FN) that update on different rules -- and why that split is exactly what makes timestomping detectable.
objectives: Explain why the $SI/$FN split makes timestomping structurally detectable
Recognize copy inheritance as the primary false positive and how MFTECmd separates it
Interpret the SI<FN, Copied, and uSecZeros indicators
Explain why $SI Accessed is unreliable on most modern systems

lessons.title: Artifact: USN Journal
lessons.summary: The append-only change log that survives even when the $MFT record it's describing gets rewritten -- reason codes, and why it's the corroborating source of first resort.
objectives: Explain the state-versus-events distinction between $MFT and the USN journal
Identify BASIC_INFO_CHANGE as the timestomping corroboration signal
Explain why the journal must be collected early because it wraps
Explain why $MFT must be parsed alongside $J to resolve paths

lessons.title: Artifact: Amcache
lessons.summary: First-execution evidence with a SHA-1 hash attached -- and the specific ways it disagrees with Prefetch that tell you something real.
objectives: Identify the SHA-1 hash as Amcache's unique investigative value
Explain why an Amcache entry establishes presence rather than execution
Reconcile disagreements between Prefetch, Amcache, and ShimCache
Collect Amcache.hve correctly including its transaction logs

lessons.title: Artifact: Shimcache
lessons.summary: Evidence of presence, not necessarily execution -- the nuance that trips up almost everyone the first time they use this artifact in a report.
objectives: Explain what the ShimCache timestamp actually represents
Explain why modern ShimCache proves presence rather than execution
Explain the shutdown-flush behavior and its collection implications
Use entry ordering as a recency signal independent of timestamps

lessons.title: Artifact: Registry Hives
lessons.summary: Where the hives actually live on disk, ControlSet numbering and which one was actually live at boot, and reading raw hives from an offline image.
objectives: Locate every major hive and its on-disk path
Explain why transaction logs must be collected with each hive
Use SYSTEM\Select\Current rather than assuming ControlSet001
Explain why deleted keys are often still recoverable from hive slack

lessons.title: Artifact: ShellBags
lessons.summary: Folder-access history that survives folder deletion -- proof a user (or an attacker with that user's session) browsed to a path that no longer exists.
objectives: Explain why ShellBags survive deletion of the folder they describe
State the GUI-only limitation and why absence proves nothing
Locate ShellBag data in both UsrClass.dat and NTUSER.DAT
Explain the account-versus-person attribution nuance

lessons.title: Artifact: UserAssist
lessons.summary: GUI-launched program history with a ROT13-encoded key and a run count -- what it captures that Prefetch doesn't, and vice versa.
objectives: Explain what UserAssist captures that Prefetch does not
Recognize ROT13 encoding as legacy design rather than security
State what UserAssist does not record and why that scopes its use
Interpret a Prefetch entry with no matching UserAssist entry

lessons.title: Event Log Key IDs Reference
lessons.summary: The Event IDs worth memorizing cold -- 4624/4625, 4688, 7045, 4104 -- and what each one actually guarantees versus merely suggests.
objectives: Interpret 4624 correctly using its Logon Type field
Explain why 4688 requires separate command-line auditing to be useful
Explain why 1102 survives the log clearing it records
Recognize 4648 explicit credential use as a lateral movement signal

lessons.title: Baseline Process Trees
lessons.summary: What a normal parent-child chain looks like for the processes attackers abuse most (services.exe, explorer.exe spawning shells) -- the baseline every 'weird process tree' red flag in this academy is measured against.
objectives: Reproduce the Windows boot process chain from System through explorer.exe
Explain why orphaned processes like explorer.exe and csrss.exe are expected
Explain why parent PID alone cannot establish lineage without creation times
Identify the highest-value tree anomalies including lsass children and misparented svchost

lessons.title: Discovery: Recognizing Attacker Recon
lessons.summary: The five Windows-native commands worth recognizing on sight, and why the pattern of several run together matters more than any single one.
objectives: Name the five most common Windows-native discovery commands and their ATT&CK mappings
Explain why a single discovery command in a log is rarely suspicious on its own
Identify what makes nltest /domain_trusts higher-signal than the other four
Explain why Discovery is iterative and how that helps scope lateral movement

lessons.title: LOLBin Catalog
lessons.summary: Five Microsoft-signed, legitimate binaries attackers proxy execution through — and the argument/parent-process patterns that separate abuse from normal use.
objectives: Name the five most commonly abused LOLBins and their ATT&CK sub-techniques
Explain the Squiblydoo technique and why it evades file-based detection
Identify the specific red-flag argument and parent-process patterns for each binary
Locate the LOLBAS project as the canonical reference beyond this lesson's five

lessons.title: BYOVD & the LOLDrivers Catalog
lessons.summary: Legitimately signed, genuinely vulnerable drivers attackers exploit for kernel-mode code execution — usually to kill EDR and antivirus outright.
objectives: Explain why signature enforcement alone doesn't stop a BYOVD attack
Explain why BYOVD is a privilege-escalation technique, not initial access
Identify the red-flag load locations and known-abused drivers for BYOVD
Name Sysmon Event ID 6 as the primary detection surface and HVCI as the primary prevention

lessons.title: Local Privilege Escalation
lessons.summary: Unquoted service paths, weak service permissions, and token impersonation — turning a low-privilege foothold into SYSTEM before AD is ever touched.
objectives: Explain how an unquoted service path can be hijacked for privilege escalation
Describe how the Potato exploit family abuses SeImpersonatePrivilege
Explain why token-impersonation escalation leaves no single dedicated alert event
Connect local privilege escalation to the Discovery and LOLBin activity it typically precedes

lessons.title: VSS Deletion: The Ransomware Precursor
lessons.summary: The attacker's side of Volume Shadow Copy — deliberately destroying the recovery option right before encryption, and the exact commands that give it away.
objectives: Name the five native Windows tools used to inhibit system recovery
Distinguish the explicit-deletion pattern from the stealthier shadow-storage-resize variant
Explain why this is primarily a prevention/early-detection topic, not a post-incident one
Explain the typical timing relationship between T1490 and T1486 in a ransomware timeline

levels.title: PowerShell & Persistence
levels.tagline: How attackers stay, and the one tool most of them use to do it.
levels.description: PowerShell is how most modern intrusions execute fileless, in memory -- and persistence is how they survive a reboot or a password reset. This level covers decoding what PowerShell actually ran, then the endpoint and cloud mechanisms that keep attackers coming back.

lessons.title: PowerShell Logging
lessons.summary: Module logging, script block logging, and transcription -- three different log sources capturing three different slices of what actually ran, and why you usually need more than one turned on.
objectives: Name the three PowerShell logging sources and what distinct slice of activity each one captures
Explain why Script Block Logging (4104) defeats most obfuscation automatically, without additional decoding
Locate PSReadLine's console history file and explain what makes it different from the event log sources
Identify the GPO settings that must be explicitly enabled before this evidence exists, and why their absence is itself a finding

lessons.title: Obfuscation & Decoding
lessons.summary: -EncodedCommand, compression layers, and string-reassembly tricks decoded step by step -- the exact skill that turns an unreadable blob into a readable command.
objectives: Decode a Base64/UTF-16LE -EncodedCommand payload by hand and explain why the encoding step is separate from any obfuscation layered on top of it
Recognize compression, string-reconstruction, and framework-based (Invoke-Obfuscation-style) obfuscation patterns at a glance
Explain why Script Block Logging often makes manual decoding unnecessary, and when manual decoding is still required
Identify the command-line truncation limitation in process-creation logging and the log source that avoids it

lessons.title: Evasion Detection
lessons.summary: AMSI bypass patterns and the logging gaps attackers specifically target -- recognized at the detection-signature level, not built.
objectives: Explain what AMSI is and at what point in PowerShell's execution pipeline it gets invoked
Recognize the canonical reflection-based AMSI bypass pattern in a decoded script block
Explain why -ExecutionPolicy Bypass is not a security boundary, and what it actually controls
Identify a PowerShell v2 downgrade attempt and explain what logging capability it specifically evades

lessons.title: Malicious Cmdlet Patterns
lessons.summary: The specific cmdlets and argument patterns that show up in real intrusions constantly enough to be worth pattern-matching on sight.
objectives: Recognize the download-cradle pattern (IEX combined with DownloadString/DownloadFile) and explain why it leaves so little on disk
Name the specific Set-MpPreference/Add-MpPreference cmdlets used to tamper with Defender, and why they're a high-confidence indicator
Explain how PowerShell's automation engine can execute without a powershell.exe process ever appearing in process-creation logs
Distinguish an individually-benign flag (like -NoProfile) from the same flag appearing as part of a suspicious cluster

lessons.title: Persistence: Registry Run Keys
lessons.summary: The oldest, still most common persistence mechanism -- Run/RunOnce, and the baseline of what's normally there versus what isn't.
objectives: Name the four primary Run/RunOnce key paths including HKCU and HKLM
Explain why RunOnce both helps and hinders an investigator
Use a Run key's LastWriteTime to date a persistence installation
Distinguish legitimate vendor entries from attacker-planted ones

lessons.title: Persistence: Scheduled Tasks
lessons.summary: Task Scheduler as an attacker's cron -- where the evidence lives beyond just `schtasks /query`.
objectives: Locate scheduled task evidence in all three places it exists
Explain how deleting the SD registry value hides a task that still runs
Identify TaskScheduler 106 as more reliably available than Security 4698
Recognize root-folder placement and interpreter actions as red flags

lessons.title: Persistence: Windows Services
lessons.summary: A malicious service dressed up to look legitimate -- what actually distinguishes it from the 200 real ones on any given host.
objectives: Explain why ServiceDll must be read for svchost-hosted services
Identify Event ID 7045 as a default-enabled service installation record
Explain why 7045 doubles as a lateral-movement detection
Interpret the Start and Type registry values including the kernel-driver case

lessons.title: Persistence: WMI Event Subscriptions
lessons.summary: Fileless, triggered-by-event persistence that survives a full disk wipe of the file it originally came from.
objectives: Name the three objects required for a WMI subscription to fire
Explain why deleting the dropper does not remove this persistence
Name the Sysmon and native event IDs covering subscription registration
Explain why legitimate management tooling makes existence the wrong baseline question

lessons.title: Persistence: COM & DLL Hijacking
lessons.summary: Redirecting a trusted lookup path so legitimate software loads an attacker's code -- and why it's so hard to spot from the process tree alone.
objectives: Explain why HKCU CLSID entries override machine-wide COM registrations
Explain why process-creation logging is blind to this technique class
Distinguish search order hijacking, phantom DLL hijacking, and side-loading
Identify Sysmon Event ID 7 as the required detection source

lessons.title: Persistence: AppInit_DLLs & IFEO
lessons.summary: Two older but still-live mechanisms for forcing code to load into every process, or hijacking a debugger key to redirect execution entirely.
objectives: Explain what an IFEO Debugger value does to program execution
Describe the accessibility backdoor and why pre-authentication reachability matters
Explain why AppInit_DLLs remains worth checking despite being disabled by default
Recognize IFEO used for defence evasion rather than persistence

lessons.title: Persistence: LSA Provider / SSP Abuse
lessons.summary: Registering a malicious security package that gets loaded directly into LSASS -- persistence with credential-theft built in for free.
objectives: Explain why a malicious SSP delivers persistence and credential theft together
Recall the known-good Security Packages baseline and audit against it
Explain why a registry-only check misses the memory-injected SSP variant
Explain how LSA Protection blocks both variants and what event it generates

lessons.title: Persistence: BITS Jobs
lessons.summary: Background Intelligent Transfer Service repurposed as a stealthy, throttled download-and-persist channel.
objectives: Explain why BITS transfers obscure attribution of network activity
Identify SetNotifyCmdLine as the option converting a download job into persistence
Locate the BITS queue database and explain why autorun-focused triage misses it
Explain why the /allusers flag is required when enumerating jobs

lessons.title: Persistence: Winlogon Shell/Userinit
lessons.summary: Hijacking the two registry values that fire on every single logon, before most endpoint monitoring has fully initialized.
objectives: State the exact correct values of Userinit and Shell
Explain why attackers append rather than replace these values
Explain why Winlogon execution timing favours the attacker
Recognize HKCU Winlogon overrides missed by an HKLM-only check

lessons.title: Persistence: OAuth Consent Grants
lessons.summary: Standing access that survives a password reset entirely -- because it was never a password to begin with.
objectives: Explain why a password reset does not revoke OAuth-granted access
Identify offline_access as the scope that converts access into persistence
Distinguish delegated from application permissions and why the latter is more serious
State the three remediation steps required to fully terminate a grant

lessons.title: Persistence: Backdoor App Registrations
lessons.summary: A malicious app registration hiding among hundreds of legitimate ones -- what actually distinguishes it on inspection.
objectives: Explain why adding a credential to an existing app is stealthier than creating one
Use credential-versus-application creation dates as the detection tell
Identify the application permissions that enable self-escalation to Global Admin
Explain why application permissions survive all user credential resets

lessons.title: Persistence: Mailbox Forwarding Rules
lessons.summary: The single most common BEC persistence mechanism -- a configuration change that survives being locked out of the account entirely.
objectives: Check all three forwarding layers rather than inbox rules alone
Recognize the forward-plus-conceal pattern characteristic of BEC
Detect hidden MAPI-layer rules invisible to Outlook
Explain why forwarding rules survive account containment

lessons.title: Persistence: Golden SAML
lessons.summary: Forging SAML assertions with a stolen federation signing certificate -- access that doesn't touch Entra ID's own authentication path at all.
objectives: Explain what the token-signing certificate enables an attacker to forge
Identify the Entra-sign-in-without-ADFS-event detection signal
Explain why MFA enforcement and password resets are ineffective
Explain why the signing certificate must be rotated twice

lessons.title: Persistence: Break-Glass Account Abuse
lessons.summary: Turning the emergency-access account meant to save you during an outage into the attacker's own permanent backdoor.
objectives: Explain why break-glass accounts are deliberately excluded from Conditional Access
Identify sign-in alerting as the control that makes them safe to maintain
Recognize exclusion-list modification as the durable attacker variant
Explain why break-glass accounts should be cloud-only

lessons.title: Non-PowerShell Execution Engines
lessons.summary: VBScript, JScript, and WMI as execution mechanisms attackers use specifically to route around PowerShell-focused logging.
objectives: Explain why an attacker would choose VBScript/JScript over PowerShell in a well-logged environment
Identify the red-flag parent-process and execution-location patterns for wscript.exe/cscript.exe
Describe how WMI can be used for direct remote command execution
Name the log source that captures WMI activity independent of standard process-creation logging

levels.title: Active Directory & Domain Controllers
levels.tagline: Domain compromise: the techniques, and the double-reset discipline that actually recovers from them.
levels.description: From NTDS.dit and replication metadata as raw evidence, through the credential-theft and ticket-forgery techniques that define domain compromise, to the delegation and certificate-services abuse paths that let a low-privilege account become Domain Admin.

lessons.title: Artifact: NTDS.dit
lessons.summary: The database holding every domain credential -- how it's actually extracted (and why doing so live is itself a red flag), and what the extraction methods themselves leave behind.
objectives: Explain why NTDS.dit extraction requires the SYSTEM registry hive alongside the database
Name the main extraction methods (shadow copy, ntdsutil IFM, secretsdump) and the trace each leaves
Explain why any extraction on a live production DC warrants investigation regardless of context
Explain why confirmed extraction makes the krbtgt double reset mandatory rather than precautionary

lessons.title: Artifact: SYSVOL & GPO Abuse
lessons.summary: Group Policy as a domain-wide code execution mechanism -- and how to tell a legitimate GPO change from one that just pushed a backdoor to every machine in an OU.
objectives: Explain why SYSVOL is readable by every authenticated domain user and what that implies
Describe how write access to a linked GPO becomes domain-wide code execution
Explain why MS14-025 did not fully resolve the GPP cpassword exposure
Use GPO version-number mismatches between the directory and SYSVOL halves as a tamper signal

lessons.title: Artifact: Replication Metadata
lessons.summary: Every object's own "last changed, by whom, from where" history baked into AD itself -- corroborating evidence that doesn't depend on logging being turned on.
objectives: Explain why replication metadata survives Security log clearing
Interpret version number, originating DSA, and originating change time for an attribute
Identify the originating-DSA anomaly that exposes DCShadow
Explain why this is corroborating rather than primary evidence

lessons.title: krbtgt & the Double Reset
lessons.summary: Why resetting the krbtgt password once doesn't invalidate a Golden Ticket, and the specific two-reset sequence, with the right wait between them, that actually does.
objectives: Explain why a single krbtgt reset leaves an existing Golden Ticket valid
State the recommended wait between resets and explain what that interval corresponds to
Distinguish the maintenance reset strategy from emergency breach recovery, and the tradeoff each carries
Explain why replication health must be verified before the first reset

lessons.title: DCSync Detection
lessons.summary: An attacker's own domain controller impersonating a real one to request every credential hash via legitimate replication traffic -- and the Event ID that's specifically designed to catch it.
objectives: Explain how DCSync obtains credentials without ever touching NTDS.dit as a file
Name the three replication extended rights that make DCSync possible
Identify Event ID 4662 with replication GUIDs as the core detection, and what distinguishes malicious from legitimate
Explain why DCSync can run from any domain-joined machine rather than requiring DC access

lessons.title: Golden Ticket / Silver Ticket
lessons.summary: Forged Kerberos tickets built from a stolen krbtgt or service-account hash -- domain-wide access, or single-service access, that bypasses normal authentication entirely.
objectives: Explain why a Golden Ticket survives password resets of the impersonated account
Distinguish Golden from Silver Tickets by key used, scope, and whether a DC is contacted
Explain why a 4769 with no preceding 4768 is a forged-ticket indicator
Identify RC4 encryption in an AES environment as a common forging tell

lessons.title: AdminSDHolder / SDProp Abuse
lessons.summary: A protection mechanism for privileged-group permissions, repurposed by attackers into a self-healing backdoor that reverts every hour.
objectives: Explain what SDProp does and its default 60-minute interval
Explain how modifying AdminSDHolder's ACL creates a self-healing backdoor
Recognize a permission reappearing after roughly an hour as an AdminSDHolder signal
Use orphaned adminCount=1 values as a historical privilege trail

lessons.title: Kerberoasting
lessons.summary: Requesting a service ticket for any account with an SPN, then cracking it offline -- no elevated privilege required to start the attack.
objectives: Explain why any authenticated domain user can begin a Kerberoasting attack
Explain why the offline cracking phase is invisible to domain-side controls
Identify the RC4 downgrade request as a detection signal
Explain why gMSAs effectively neutralize the attack

lessons.title: AD CS Abuse (ESC1/ESC4/ESC8)
lessons.summary: Misconfigured certificate templates as a domain-admin escalation path that most environments have never audited -- the three most common misconfiguration classes explained concretely.
objectives: Explain why a stolen certificate survives password resets and requires revocation instead
Identify the four conditions that make a template ESC1-vulnerable
Explain why ESC4 can evade a point-in-time template audit
Trace the ESC8 path from NTLM relay to a DC certificate to DCSync
Name the Certificate Services event IDs relevant to detection

lessons.title: ACL & Delegation Abuse
lessons.summary: Legitimate-looking delegated permissions (reset password, write to a group) chained together into a full privilege-escalation path -- the kind of attack that never touches a single exploit.
objectives: Explain why WriteDacl and WriteOwner are equivalent to full control
Explain why access reviews structurally miss chained ACL escalation paths
Define a shadow admin and why membership-based reviews miss them
Recognize servicePrincipalName writes as GenericWrite converted into a Kerberoasting opportunity

lessons.title: Pass-the-Hash / Pass-the-Ticket
lessons.summary: Reusing a stolen NTLM hash or Kerberos ticket directly for lateral movement — no password cracking, no privileged access required to start.
objectives: Explain why Pass the Hash works without the attacker knowing the cleartext password
Distinguish Pass the Hash from Pass the Ticket by credential type used
Define overpass-the-hash and explain how it bridges the two techniques
Identify the log correlation pattern that most reliably surfaces either technique

lessons.title: Kerberos Delegation Abuse
lessons.summary: Unconstrained, constrained, and resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD) — abusing a legitimate Kerberos feature to reach the same outcome as a forged ticket.
objectives: Distinguish unconstrained, constrained, and resource-based constrained delegation
Explain the full RBCD attack chain from GenericWrite to impersonating a Domain Admin
Identify the specific attributes and events that surface delegation abuse
Name the mitigations (Protected Users, NOT_DELEGATED, MachineAccountQuota) that prevent it

lessons.title: NTLM Relay
lessons.summary: Forwarding a live authentication attempt to an unintended destination — no cracking, no hash theft, just exploiting NTLM's failure to bind authentication to a target.
objectives: Explain the core NTLM design flaw that makes relay possible
Describe the three-part chain: coercion/poisoning, relay tooling, and an unsigned target
Identify the two signing controls that make the entire relay chain fail regardless of earlier steps
Explain how NTLM relay can lead directly into RBCD abuse

lessons.title: The AD Attack Chain: Putting It Together
lessons.summary: Every AD technique in this level, in the order they actually chain together — with a diagram walking foothold to domain compromise.
objectives: Sequence the seven stages of a typical AD attack chain and what each stage produces for the next
Explain why the chain represents a common shape rather than a fixed script
Use the chain as an investigative tool for scoping evidence around a single found artifact
Explain why recovery scope depends on how far an intrusion travelled through the chain

levels.title: Windows Memory Forensics
levels.tagline: What only exists while the machine is running -- and disappears the moment it's powered off.
levels.description: Acquisition through triage: process/thread internals, code injection techniques and how to actually find them in a memory image, and the network artifacts that survive in RAM even when the connection itself is long closed.

lessons.title: Acquisition
lessons.summary: Getting a forensically sound memory image off a live, running system -- the tools, and what "sound" actually requires here.
objectives: Explain why RAM acquisition necessarily changes the system being acquired, and what "forensically sound" requires as a result
Name at least three live acquisition tools and one situation where each would be preferred
Explain what hiberfil.sys and a crash dump each provide as cold, alternate memory sources
Explain why a hypervisor-side VM snapshot can be preferable to an in-guest acquisition tool

lessons.title: Process Analysis
lessons.summary: Volatility's process-listing plugins and what a hidden or unlinked process actually looks like once you know where to look.
objectives: Explain why pslist and psscan should always be run as a pair, and what a mismatch between them means
Explain what ldrmodules adds beyond what dlllist alone shows
Explain why cmdline recovery from memory is valuable even when process-creation logging was enabled
Name the Volatility 3 plugins for process listing, tree view, command-line recovery, and handle enumeration

lessons.title: EPROCESS Internals
lessons.summary: The kernel structure every process-listing plugin is actually walking -- and why understanding it explains why DKOM hiding works at all.
objectives: Explain why InheritedFromUniqueProcessId alone cannot prove a live parent-child relationship
Explain how DKOM hides a process from enumeration without stopping it from running
Explain why psscan defeats DKOM hiding when pslist does not
Identify what the PEB pointer in an EPROCESS structure leads to and why it matters

lessons.title: Injected Code Detection
lessons.summary: Finding code that was never loaded from a legitimate file on disk -- the memory-region characteristics that give it away.
objectives: Name the three co-occurring properties malfind looks for in a flagged memory region
Explain what a VAD is and how malfind relates to it
Recognize JIT compilation as a common, legitimate cause of malfind false positives and how to distinguish it from real injection
Explain why the same malfind finding carries different weight depending on which process it appears in

lessons.title: Injection Techniques
lessons.summary: Process hollowing, DLL injection, and the other major techniques for running attacker code inside a legitimate process's address space.
objectives: Identify the memory signature of process hollowing versus classic DLL injection
Explain why reflective DLL injection doesn't appear in a process's normal module list
Explain what makes the "Early Bird" APC injection variant specifically effective at evasion
Distinguish thread execution hijacking from techniques that create a new thread

lessons.title: Thread Analysis
lessons.summary: A thread with no backing module, or a start address that doesn't correspond to any loaded code -- one of the cleanest injection tells there is.
objectives: Explain what a thread start address in private, unbacked memory indicates
Explain why a persistently suspended thread is worth flagging even though suspension itself is normal
Identify a mid-function start-address offset as a distinct injection tell
Explain how thread-level analysis complements process- and memory-region-level findings

lessons.title: Mutex (Mutant) Analysis
lessons.summary: Malware families that name their own mutex, sometimes literally to prevent re-infecting the same machine -- a naming pattern that becomes a searchable indicator.
objectives: Explain why malware families commonly create a mutex with a hardcoded, distinctive name
Explain why a mutex name can be a more durable indicator than a file hash
Identify "Mutant" as the underlying Windows kernel term for a mutex
Explain why the mere presence of a named mutex is not itself a red flag

lessons.title: LSASS Memory Analysis
lessons.summary: Where Windows keeps live credential material in memory, and the specific access patterns (not just "LSASS was touched") that separate credential theft from normal system activity.
objectives: Explain the condition under which WDigest can cache plaintext-recoverable credentials
Explain why "LSASS was accessed" is the wrong question, and what actually distinguishes theft from routine access
Explain what LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) specifically prevents, and why BYOVD exists partly as a response to it
Name at least three distinct LSASS-dumping methods, including the LOLBin variant

lessons.title: Network Artifacts in Memory
lessons.summary: Connection state that outlives the connection itself -- what's still recoverable in RAM after a C2 channel has already closed.
objectives: Explain why a closed network connection can still be recoverable from a memory image
Explain what the Owner field in netscan output adds when correlated against other findings in this level
Relate netscan's recovery of closed connections to the DKOM/psscan concept from earlier in this level
Explain why a recovered remote address should be checked against C2 fingerprinting content rather than judged in isolation

lessons.title: Malware Triage Methodology
lessons.summary: Putting the whole memory module together into an actual triage sequence -- what to check first, and when to stop and escalate to full reverse engineering instead.
objectives: Sequence a full memory triage from acquisition verification through fingerprinting in the correct order
Explain why LSASS is checked as its own dedicated step rather than only as a follow-up to other findings
Distinguish what memory triage answers from what requires full reverse engineering
Identify at least two concrete signals that indicate a triage should escalate to reverse engineering

levels.title: Email Forensics, Hybrid Response & Microsoft Defender
levels.tagline: A mailbox, a hybrid identity, and the endpoint security product doing the most work on every host in this academy's scope.
levels.description: The hybrid account-compromise runbook this academy is built around, email header/message forensics, and Microsoft Defender's antivirus and endpoint-protection mechanics -- how it operates, mitigates, quarantines, and what an attempt to evade or disable it looks like forensically. Deep Entra/Conditional Access/hybrid-sync investigation now lives in a separate cloud-DFIR project; this level keeps only what's genuinely hybrid or endpoint-adjacent.

lessons.title: Cloud Identity Overview & Hybrid Account-Compromise Runbook
lessons.summary: The core hybrid recovery discipline this academy keeps coming back to: why the password has to be reset twice, and why PowerShell's session revocation does something the GUI simply can't.
objectives: Explain why a single password reset leaves existing refresh tokens valid
State exactly what Revoke-MgUserSignInSession invalidates that a GUI-only reset does not
Explain why hybrid (AD-synced) accounts specifically require resetting the password twice
Sequence a full hybrid account-compromise response in the correct order

lessons.title: Email Headers & Authentication Forensics
lessons.summary: Reading the Received chain, the From/Reply-To/Return-Path spoofing triangle, and what SPF/DKIM/DMARC each actually prove -- plus reading Microsoft 365's own compauth verdict directly.
objectives: Read a Received chain bottom-up and identify the trust boundary
Distinguish From, Return-Path, and Reply-To and the spoofing triangle they form
Explain why SPF pass does not mean not-spoofed, and what DMARC alignment adds
Interpret Microsoft 365 composite authentication results

lessons.title: Message Source & Attachment Forensics
lessons.summary: Parsing raw MIME structure, hashing attachments before opening them, and the HTML-vs-plaintext mismatch that's still one of the most reliable phishing tells in active use.
objectives: Parse MIME structure and identify plain-text versus HTML mismatches
Recognize double extensions, RTL override, and container-format delivery
Hash and extract attachments safely before any analysis
Identify PST, OST, and MBOX offline formats and when the OST is the only surviving copy

lessons.title: Defender AV & MDE: Core Mechanics
lessons.summary: The three protection layers, passive vs. active mode, and the 1116/1117 detection-and-action event pair that anchors most Defender-driven timelines.
objectives: Name the three protection layers and which one intercepts fileless, in-memory activity specifically
Interpret a 1116 event with no matching 1117 remediation correctly
Distinguish passive mode from active mode and why it changes how you read the event pair
Explain why zero detection history across a fleet is itself worth investigating

lessons.title: Attack Surface Reduction & Tamper Protection
lessons.summary: The named rule that blocks LSASS credential theft directly, the 1121/1122 block-vs-audit event pair, and why Tamper Protection is built to resist even a local administrator.
objectives: Name the ASR rule that directly protects the LSASS-access surface covered in Level 5
Distinguish what a 1121 event confirms versus what a 1122 event only suggests
Explain why Tamper Protection specifically targets the local-administrator threat model
Recognize the exclusion-added-right-after-a-block pattern as deliberate evasion

lessons.title: Automated Investigation, Remediation & Live Response
lessons.summary: Quarantine mechanics, what AIR actually automates, the September 2026 change that folded it into always-on antivirus, and Live Response as the manual complement.
objectives: Explain why a quarantined file requires a decoding tool like DeXRAY before it can be analyzed further
State what changed for AIR specifically on September 1, 2026, and what stayed the same
Explain why Microsoft's own guidance advises against the "no automation" AIR level
Identify Live Response as a manual, auditable complement to AIR's automation

lessons.title: Observable Evasion & Bypass Techniques
lessons.summary: What an attempt to disable, blind, or route around Defender looks like forensically -- PowerShell tampering, BYOVD as EDR-blinding, registry-based disabling, and Tamper Protection bypass attempts, tied back to Level 2 and Level 3.
objectives: Distinguish kernel-level EDR-blinding (BYOVD) from user-mode tampering, and why Tamper Protection only stops the latter
Explain why a silent gap in Defender's log is a stronger signal than a logged 5001 disable event
Identify the registry-based disabling route as a separate blind spot from PowerShell-focused monitoring
Explain why a failed tampering attempt against a Tamper-Protected host still warrants full investigation

lessons.title: Advanced Hunting with KQL
lessons.summary: Querying Defender's Device* tables directly (DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceNetworkEvents, DeviceFileEvents, DeviceRegistryEvents, DeviceImageLoadEvents) -- the query patterns that come up constantly enough to memorize.
objectives: Select the correct Device* table for a given detection question
Write filter-first KQL and explain why ordering matters for performance
Apply the memorizable query patterns for Office-spawned shells and encoded PowerShell
Use prevalence counting to find anomalies without a prior signature

lessons.title: Detection Engineering
lessons.summary: Turning a one-off endpoint hunt query into a standing Sigma-style detection rule that fires automatically on the next occurrence.
objectives: Walk the detection lifecycle and identify the steps teams usually skip
Explain why an untuned rule is worse than no rule
Scope exclusions narrowly and document them with review dates
Explain the portability argument for writing detections in Sigma

lessons.title: Defender for Identity Mapping
lessons.summary: Mapping Defender for Identity's own alert catalog back onto the AD attack techniques earlier in this academy -- DCSync and Golden Ticket both have a specific alert name to know.
objectives: Explain what DC-level sensors detect that endpoint EDR cannot
Map Defender for Identity alert concepts onto Level 4 techniques
Explain why honeytoken activity is actionable without correlation
Explain why an alert does not replace understanding the technique

levels.title: Network Forensics & Anti-Forensics
levels.tagline: What crossed the wire, and what happens when the attacker tries to make sure you never find out.
levels.description: Log- and flow-level network evidence (deliberately scoped short of full packet capture -- that's its own discipline), then the anti-forensic techniques attackers use to cover their tracks, and how much of that cleanup is actually reversible.

lessons.title: DNS Analysis
lessons.summary: Tunneling, domain generation algorithms, and beaconing patterns -- all visible in query logs alone, no packet capture required.
objectives: Identify DNS tunnelling by query length, entropy, record type, and volume
Recognize the NXDOMAIN signature of a domain generation algorithm
Explain why jitter fails to conceal beaconing from inter-arrival analysis
Explain why Sysmon Event ID 22 changes what DNS data can prove

lessons.title: Proxy & Firewall Log Triage
lessons.summary: Reading a connection log for what actually matters: user-agent mismatches, beaconing intervals, byte-ratio anomalies, and TLS fingerprinting.
objectives: Interpret byte-ratio patterns to distinguish browsing, beaconing, and exfiltration
Recognize library-default User-Agents as client-identifying indicators
Explain why a JA3 fingerprint is more durable than an IP or domain
Use destination rarity and domain age as prevalence-based triage signals

lessons.title: NetFlow & Flow-Record Analysis
lessons.summary: Connection metadata at scale -- who talked to whom, how much, for how long -- cheap enough to retain for months where full packet capture rarely is.
objectives: Explain why flow retention often beats PCAP detail in practice
Identify east-west workstation-to-workstation traffic as lateral movement
Explain the perimeter-only collection blind spot
State precisely what flow data can and cannot establish about exfiltration

lessons.title: C2 Framework Fingerprinting
lessons.summary: JA3/JA3S/JA4 TLS fingerprinting, named pipe indicators, and the behavioral tells that survive a Malleable C2 profile — identifying which C2 framework is behind a beaconing pattern.
objectives: Explain what JA3/JA3S/JA4 fingerprint and why Malleable profiles don't defeat them
Identify Cobalt Strike's default named pipe patterns and the Sysmon events that capture them
Describe the beacon-rhythm behavioral signature that survives any network disguise
Explain why fingerprinting should be one signal among several, not relied on alone

lessons.title: File Carving
lessons.summary: Recovering files from unallocated space by content signature alone, after the filesystem's own record of them is gone.
objectives: Explain how header/footer signature carving works without the filesystem
Explain why fragmentation is the defining limitation of carving
Prefer MFT-record recovery over carving when the record survives
Recognize resident storage as a third recovery path for small files

lessons.title: Alternate Data Streams
lessons.summary: NTFS's own hidden-storage feature, invisible to Explorer and `dir` by default -- a genuine blind spot most casual triage never checks.
objectives: Explain how a named stream conceals content without changing reported file size
Use Zone.Identifier as origin evidence, including what its absence implies
Explain why container formats became a MOTW-stripping delivery path
Detect streams with dir /R, PowerShell, and Sysmon Event ID 15

lessons.title: Log & Artifact Recovery
lessons.summary: What survives after an attacker clears the Security event log -- because "cleared" and "unrecoverable" are not the same thing.
objectives: Explain why 1102 cannot be suppressed by repeated clearing
Recover event records by carving EVTX structures from unallocated space
Explain why Windows Event Forwarding inverts the value of log clearing
Enumerate the non-log artifact set unaffected by log clearing

lessons.title: Volume Shadow Copy Recovery
lessons.summary: Windows' own built-in point-in-time backups, and what they preserve even after files are deleted or a ransomware note appears.
objectives: Explain copy-on-write and what a shadow copy actually stores
Use a pre-intrusion hive diff to produce a persistence inventory
Explain why bulk shadow copy deletion is a high-confidence indicator
State the limitations that prevent relying on snapshot history

lessons.title: Memory-Based File Recovery
lessons.summary: Recovering a file's actual content from RAM when it was deliberately never written to disk at all.
objectives: Explain why memory is the only recovery path for filesystem-avoiding artifacts
Use malfind --dump and dumpfiles to extract payloads from memory
Explain why encrypted-at-rest files can be recovered in plaintext
Characterize memory-recovered content correctly in reporting

levels.title: Capstone: Playbooks & Case Studies
levels.tagline: Everything above, run end to end against a realistic scenario.
levels.description: Investigation playbooks by scenario type, two full case studies worked start to finish, and the practice drills that put specific artifacts from earlier levels under real time pressure.

lessons.title: Case Study: Domain Compromise, End to End
lessons.summary: Every technique from Level 4, chained together into one realistic intrusion narrative from initial foothold to Domain Admin.
objectives: Trace a full intrusion from phishing through Golden Ticket using the artifacts at each stage
Explain why 4662 firing correctly did not prevent the compromise
Evaluate the staged-versus-rapid krbtgt reset decision in context
Identify cloud persistence as the gap an on-premises remediation plan missed

lessons.title: Case Study: Business Email Compromise, End to End
lessons.summary: A single compromised mailbox, followed through mailbox rules, OAuth grants, and outbound fraud -- the email and cloud-identity levels applied together.
objectives: Explain why MFA did not prevent an illicit consent grant
Explain why the immediate password reset failed to terminate access
Explain why the fraudulent message passed all email authentication checks
Identify the single tenant setting that would have removed the attack surface

lessons.title: Playbook: Business Email Compromise
lessons.summary: Trigger through lessons-learned for a BEC engagement specifically -- what to pull, in what order, and when it's actually contained.
objectives: Sequence BEC containment so session revocation accompanies the password reset
Check for attacker-registered MFA methods as part of initial containment
Use MailItemsAccessed to make a defensible data-exposure statement
Identify OAuth grants as persistence that survives credential rotation

lessons.title: Playbook: Domain Compromise / Lateral Movement
lessons.summary: The domain-wide version of the same discipline -- scoping how far an attacker actually moved before you can honestly call it contained.
objectives: Explain why scoping precedes remediation here, and the one stated exception
Assemble the coordinated remediation event in the correct order
Explain why certificate revocation must be included alongside credential rotation
Articulate what makes the rebuild-versus-remediate decision answerable

lessons.title: Playbook: Ransomware
lessons.summary: The playbook that has to run under the most time pressure of any in this academy, with recovery decisions that can't wait for a complete investigation first.
objectives: Explain why encryption marks the end of an intrusion and what that implies for scoping
Choose network isolation over power-off and justify the tradeoff
Explain why exfiltration determination belongs in the first hour
Explain why restoring before identifying initial access risks re-encryption

lessons.title: Playbook: Insider Threat
lessons.summary: A fundamentally different investigative posture -- the subject already had legitimate access, so "how did they get in" isn't the question.
objectives: Reframe the investigative question around exceeded authorization rather than intrusion
Explain why baseline establishment must precede review of the subject's activity
Explain why access-revocation timing is coordinated with HR and Legal
Explain why documenting what was not found matters in this playbook specifically

lessons.title: Playbook: Data Exfiltration
lessons.summary: Proving what actually left, not just what could have -- and why that distinction matters enormously for breach-notification scope.
objectives: Distinguish access from exfiltration, including the FileAccessed/FileDownloaded case
Prioritize short-retention egress log collection in the first hour
Produce a three-tier scope statement with stated confidence and gaps
Explain why encrypted egress remains analyzable by volume and destination

lessons.title: Playbook: Phishing (Initial Access)
lessons.summary: The playbook for the most common initial-access vector of all -- and when a single phishing email needs to become an organization-wide search.
objectives: Explain why the original message rather than a forward is required
Distinguish received, opened, clicked, and submitted as four separate populations
Apply the criteria that escalate one email to an organization-wide incident
Explain why every clicker is treated as a possible submitter

lessons.title: Playbook: Web Shell / Server Compromise
lessons.summary: A different attack surface entirely -- internet-facing servers, and the specific evidence a web shell leaves that a workstation compromise doesn't.
objectives: Explain why a web shell requires no persistence mechanism or callback
Identify w3wp.exe spawning a command interpreter as a near-definitive indicator
Use IIS logs to date shell activation when the Security log does not reach
Explain why closing the write path, not deleting the shell, is the closure criterion

lessons.title: Drill: Prefetch Triage
lessons.summary: A timed, hands-on exercise applying Level 2's Prefetch lesson to a realistic triage scenario.
objectives: Identify two .pf files for one executable name as evidence of two execution paths
Use run counts and timestamp clustering to isolate a suspicious sequence
Distinguish the legitimate high-count svchost entry from the anomalous one
Determine what to extract next from the candidate .pf files

lessons.title: Drill: Process Tree Triage
lessons.summary: Spot the abnormal parent-child chain against the baseline from Level 2.
objectives: Prioritize lsass.exe with a child as the highest-value finding
Recognize the explorer.exe orphan as expected rather than anomalous
Identify both violations in a misparented svchost.exe
Explain why the Office-to-PowerShell branch is a compound indicator

lessons.title: Drill: Registry Persistence Triage
lessons.summary: Find the planted persistence mechanism among a realistic registry export.
objectives: Detect an appended path in the Winlogon Userinit value
Recognize an IFEO Debugger on an accessibility binary as a pre-authentication backdoor
Interpret service Type and Start values correctly
Explain why redundant persistence means removing one mechanism is insufficient

lessons.title: Drill: PowerShell Decode
lessons.summary: Decode an obfuscated command chain using exactly the technique from Level 3.
objectives: Decode a Base64/UTF-16LE payload including the step most people skip
Read a download cradle and explain why it leaves no disk artifact
Identify what remains unknown after decoding the first stage
Explain the configuration dependency that made the command line available at all

lessons.title: Drill: Event Log Story
lessons.summary: Reconstruct what happened on a host from Event IDs alone.
objectives: Distinguish password spraying from brute forcing by event pattern
Explain why System log events survive a Security log clear
Recognize account creation plus privileged group addition as persistence
State what authentication-only telemetry cannot establish

lessons.title: Drill: Timeline Correlation
lessons.summary: Correlate multiple sources with mismatched clocks into one coherent timeline.
objectives: Normalize sources to UTC and calibrate host clock skew separately
Use a cross-recorded event to derive a constant offset
Explain how an uncorrected source inverts a causal chain
Read a byte-ratio profile to distinguish beaconing from exfiltration

lessons.title: Certification Roadmap
lessons.summary: Mapping this academy's levels onto real GIAC certifications — GCFE, GCFA, GCIH, GNFA — and a realistic order to pursue them in.
objectives: Map GCFE, GCFA, and GCIH onto the specific academy levels each one corresponds to
Explain why GCFE is typically pursued before GCFA
Identify which academy content maps to GNFA and GCTI specifically
Determine a realistic certification sequence based on personal role and interest, not a fixed checklist

lessons.title: Practice Labs and Next Steps
lessons.summary: Real, free places to get hands-on with actual forensic evidence, and a concrete plan for what to do after finishing this academy.
objectives: Name at least three legitimate, free sources of real forensic evidence for practice
Explain why NIST CFReDS's known-answer format matters for self-directed learning
Describe the minimum lab setup needed to practice this academy's tooling
Identify a concrete next step appropriate to personal role and goals
